label: rem:reduction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:reduction}
If $k_i=n$ for some $i$, then both sides of \eqref{eq:higher-godbersen} are equal to $\frac{(n!)^p}{(pn)!}\operatorname{V}_n(K)^p$,
see \cite[Remark 3.5 (b)]{K25},
hence equality is attained for any $K$. Similarly, if $K$ is lower-dimensional, then both sides of \eqref{eq:higher-godbersen} are always equal to zero.

Furthermore, by \cite[Lemma 3.1]{FK26}, zero indices can be eliminated without changing whether equality holds. Thus, apart from the trivial cases above, it suffices to consider $k_0, \dots, k_p\geq1$, which in particular implies $p\leq n-1$.

label: prop1.6
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop1.6}
Let $1\leq p\leq n-1$ and fix integers $k_0,\dots, k_p\geq 1$ with $\sum_{i=0}^pk_i=n$. Assume $K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is a full-dimensional convex body. Then $K$ attains equality in \eqref{eq:higher-godbersen} if and only if  for any $p+1$ directions $u_0,\dots, u_{p}\in \mathbb{R}^n$ with $\dim T(K,u_i)\leq k_i$, there exists a direction $w\in \mathbb{R}^n$ such that $T(K,u_i)\subseteq T(K,w)$ for all $i=0,\dots,p$.

label: lem:minimal-face
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:minimal-face}
The face $F(K,x)$ is the unique face of $K$ containing $x$ in its relative interior.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we have  $x\in \operatorname{relint} F(K,x)$. Indeed, if $x\in \operatorname{relbd} F(K,x)$, then we may choose a proper face $G$ of  $F(K,x)$ containing $x$. Then $G$ is a face of $K$ which is strictly contained in $F(K,x)$, contradicting the definition of $F(K,x)$.
    Now we show the uniqueness. 
    Let $F'$ be any face  with $x\in \operatorname{relint} F'$. Then $x\in F(K,x)\cap F'$. The definition of $F(K,x)$ implies $F(K,x)\subseteq F'$. Therefore, $F(K,x)$ is a face of $F'$. But if $F(K,x)$ is a proper face of $F'$, then  $x\in F(K,x)\subseteq \operatorname{relbd} F'$, contradicting the choice of $F'$. Hence $F' = F(K,x)$ as desired.
head: environment

label: lemma2.1
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $x\in F\cap \operatorname{relint} G$.
For any $a\in G\setminus\{x\}$, there exists $b\in G$ such that $x\in(a,b)$.
Since $F$ is a face, we have $a,b\in F$.
Since $a$ was chosen arbitrarily in $G$, it follows that $G\subseteq F$.
head: environment

label: lemma2.2
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x\in (u,v)$ and consider $H:=F(K,x)$. Lemma \ref{lem:minimal-face} implies $x\in \operatorname{relint} H$.
Since $x\in (u,v)$, we have $u,v\in H$.
Hence by Lemma \ref{lemma2.1} we have $F,G \subseteq H$.
Since $x\in F\vee G$, we have $H = F\vee G$.
Therefore $x\in \operatorname{relint} (F\vee G)$ and the claim follows.
head: environment

label: lem:fact
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
Using the first bijection of Lemma \ref{lem:fact}, we may immediately transfer all the properties of faces to touching cones. 
For example, Lemma \ref{lem:minimal-face} implies that $u\in \operatorname{relint} T(K,u)$. In addition,  for any $v\in T(K,u)\setminus\{0\}$,  $T(K,v)$ is the face of $T(K,u)$ containing $v$ in the relative interior, cf. \cite[Lemma 2.2]{vHW25}. 
Note also that $u\in \mathbb S^{n-1}$ is a $p$-extreme direction for $K\in\mathcal{K}^n_o$ if and only if $\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}u\cap \partial K^\circ$ is a $p$-extreme point of $K^\circ$.

label: lem:exact
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \eqref{eq:mv_covariance}, for $t_1,\dots,t_m\geq0$ we have
$$
\operatorname{V}_n\left(\sum_{i=1}^m t_iK_i\right)=|\det T|\prod_{i=1}^m t_i^{d_i}\operatorname{V}_{d_i}^{E_i}(K_i).
$$
Comparing the coefficients of $t_1^{d_1}\cdots t_m^{d_m}$ proves the claim.
head: environment

label: lem2.5
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The operator $T$ block diagonalizes
$\sum_{i=1}^m t_i A_i$ for any $t_1,\dots,t_m\in\mathbb{R}$. Hence
$$
\det\left(\sum_{i=1}^ m t_iA_i\right)
=
\det\left(T^t\operatorname{diag}(t_iA_i|_{E_i})_{i=1}^ m T\right)
=
|\det T|^2\prod_{i=1}^ m t_i^{d_i}\det(A_i|_{E_i}),
$$
where $\operatorname{diag}(t_iA_i|_{E_i})_{i=1}^ m$ is the block diagonal matrix where the $i$-th block is $t_iA_i|_{E_i}$.
The conclusion  now follows by comparing coefficients.

label: cor2.9
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor2.9}
Let $E\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be an $m$-dimensional subspace, where $2\leq m\leq n$, and let $C_1,\dots,C_{m-1}\in\mathcal{K}^n$.
Let $B$ be the Euclidean unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$. 
We have
$$
\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^E_{\operatorname{P}_E C_1,\dots,\operatorname{P}_E C_{m-1}}\subseteq\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-m],C_1,\dots,C_{m-1}}.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on $n-m$, the case $n=m$ being immediate.
Suppose $n>m$ and fix $u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^E_{\operatorname{P}_E C_1,\dots,\operatorname{P}_E C_{m-1}}$.
Choose a unit vector $v\in E^\perp$.
Since $\operatorname{P}_{v^\perp}B$ is the unit ball in $v^\perp$ and $\operatorname{P}_E\operatorname{P}_{v^\perp}=\operatorname{P}_E$, the induction hypothesis gives
$$
u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^{v^\perp}_{(\operatorname{P}_{v^\perp}B)[n-m-1],\operatorname{P}_{v^\perp}C_1,\dots,\operatorname{P}_{v^\perp}C_{m-1}}.
$$
Since $T(B,u)=\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}u$ and $v\perp u$, \cite[Theorem~ 1.21]{vHW25} implies $u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-m],C_1,\dots,C_{m-1}}$.

label: lem3.1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem3.1}
    Let $K,L,C_1,\dots, C_{n-2}\in\mathcal{K}^n$. Assume $\operatorname{V}_n(L,L,C_1,\dots,C_{n-2})>0$ and
    $$
    \operatorname{V}_n(K,L,C_1,\dots, C_{n-2})^2 = \operatorname{V}_n(K,K,C_1,\dots, C_{n-2})\operatorname{V}_n(L,L,C_1,\dots, C_{n-2}).
    $$
    Then $\operatorname{S}_{K,C_1,\dots, C_{n-2}} = \alpha \operatorname{S}_{L,C_1,\dots, C_{n-2}} $
    holds with  $\alpha =\frac{\operatorname{V}_n(K,L,C_1,\dots,C_{n-2})}{\operatorname{V}_n(L,L,C_1,\dots,C_{n-2})}.$

label: lem2.11
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem2.11}
Fix an integer $1\leq k\leq n$.
Let $K,L,C_1,\dots, C_{n-k}\in\mathcal{K}^n$ be convex bodies such that $K\subseteq L$ and $\operatorname{V}_n(L[k],C_1,\dots,C_{n-k})>0$.
Denote by $B$ the unit Euclidean ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Then
$$
\operatorname{V}_n(K[ k],C_1,\ldots,C_{n- k})=\operatorname{V}_n(L[ k],C_1,\ldots,C_{n- k})
$$
    holds  if and only if
    $$
    h_K=h_L\quad\text{on}\quad\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[ k-1],C_1,\ldots,C_{n- k}}.
    $$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show the ``only if'' part by induction on $ k$.
    The base case is $ k=1$. By \eqref{eq:area-integral}, 
    $$
    \operatorname{V}_n(K,C_1,\dots,C_{n-1})-\operatorname{V}_n(L,C_1,\dots,C_{n-1})=
    \frac{1}{n}\int_{\mathbb S^{n-1}} (h_K-h_L) d\operatorname{S}_{C_1,\dots, C_{n-1}}.
    $$
    Since $K\subseteq L$, we have $h_K\leq h_L$. Therefore, the difference on the left-hand side vanishes if and only if $h_K=h_L$ on $\operatorname{supp} \operatorname{S}_{C_1,\dots, C_{n-1}}$.

    Now assume the conclusion holds for $ k-1$ and write $\mathcal C$ for the tuple $(C_1,\dots, C_{n-k}) $.
    By assumption and monotonicity of mixed volumes, we have that for all $1\leq i\leq  k-1$, 
    $  \operatorname{V}_n(K[i],L[ k-i],\mathcal C)  $
    is equal to the same positive constant.
    In particular,
    \begin{align*}        
    \operatorname{V}_n &(K,L,K[i-1],L[ k-i-1],\mathcal C)^2\\
    &=\operatorname{V}_n(K,K,K[i-1],L[ k-i-1],\mathcal C)\operatorname{V}_n(L,L,K[i-1],L[ k-i-1],\mathcal C).
    \end{align*}
    By Lemma \ref{lem3.1},  this implies $\operatorname{S}_{K,K[i-1],L[ k-i-1],\mathcal C} = \operatorname{S}_{L,K[i-1],L[ k-i-1],\mathcal C}$, and so by \eqref{eq:area-integral} we have 
    $$
    \operatorname{V}_n(K[i],L[ k-i-1], \mathcal{C}, B)=\operatorname{V}_n(K[i-1],L[ k-i], \mathcal{C}, B).
    $$
    Since this holds for all $1\leq i\leq  k-1$, we obtain $
    \operatorname{V}_n(K[ k-1], \mathcal{C}, B)=\operatorname{V}_n(L[ k-1], \mathcal{C}, B)$, and hence, by induction hypothesis, 
    $$
    h_K = h_L \quad \text{on} \quad \operatorname{supp} \operatorname{S}_{B[ k-2],\mathcal{C}, B} = \operatorname{supp} \operatorname{S}_{B[ k-1],\mathcal{C}}.
    $$
    
    For the ``if'' part, recall the following classical fact from \cite[Lemma 7.6.15]{Sch14}:
    $$
    \operatorname{supp} S_{C_1,C_2,\dots, C_{n-1}}\subseteq \operatorname{supp} S_{B, C_2,\dots, C_{n-1}}.
    $$
    This together with the assumption implies
    $$
    \operatorname{V}_n(K[ k],\mathcal C)=\operatorname{V}_n(K[ k-1],L,\mathcal C).
    $$
    Iterating the same argument then yields $\operatorname{V}_n(K[ k],\mathcal C)=\operatorname{V}_n(L[ k],\mathcal C)$.

label: lem:detP
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:detP}
For nonzero $u, v\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we have
$$
\left|\det\left(P_{u^\perp}|_{v^\perp}\right)\right|
=
\frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|}{\|u\|\|v\|}.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume $u$ and $v$ are not parallel, otherwise the claim is trivial. 
Decompose $\mathbb{R}^n = \operatorname{span}(u,v) \oplus (u^\perp\cap v^\perp)$.
The projection  $P_{u^\perp}|_{v^\perp}$ is the identity on $u^\perp\cap v^\perp$ while for $x\in v^\perp\cap \operatorname{span}(u,v)$ we have $\|P_{u^\perp}x\| =\frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|}{\|u\|\|v\|}\|x\|$. Therefore, $\left|\det\left(P_{u^\perp}|_{v^\perp}\right)\right|
= \frac{|\langle u,v\rangle|}{\|u\|\|v\|}$.
head: environment

label: lem4.1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem4.1}
Let $E\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ be a linear subspace, $C\subseteq E$ a convex body whose support function is $C^2$  on $E\setminus\{0\}$, and $u\in \mathbb S^{n-1}$ such that $P_E u\neq 0$. Consider the decomposition $u^\perp=(E\cap u^\perp)\oplus W$, where $W$ is the orthogonal complement of  $E\cap u^\perp$ inside $u^\perp$. Then
$$
D^2 h_C(u) = \frac{1}{\|P_E u\|}D^2_E h_C\left(\frac{P_E u}{\|P_E u\|}\right)\oplus \mathbf{0}_W,
$$
where $D^2_E h_C$ is first computed inside $E$ and then naturally embedded into $\mathbb{R}^n$.
head: environment

label: eq20
title: Proof
body_md:
Since $C\subseteq E$, it holds that $h_C(x) = h_C(P_E x)$. Therefore, by the chain rule and the $(-1)$-homogeneity of $\nabla^2_E h_C$,
    \begin{equation}
        \label{eq20}
    \nabla^2 h_C(u) =  P_E^t \nabla^2_E h_C(P_E u) P_E =\frac{1}{\|P_E u\|}P_E^t \nabla^2_E h_C\left(\frac{P_E u}{\|P_E u\|}\right)P_E
    \end{equation}
    where $\nabla^2_E h_C$ is the Euclidean Hessian of $h_C$ computed inside $E$.
    Now restricting \eqref{eq20} to $u^\perp$, we obtain 
    $$
    D^2h_C(u) = \frac{1}{\|P_E u\|}P_{E\cap u^\perp}^t D^2_E h_C\left(\frac{P_E u}{\|P_E u\|}\right)P_{E\cap u^\perp},
    $$
    which is exactly the desired formula.
head: environment

label: prop:local_proj
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We may assume that each $C_i$ is full-dimensional in $E_i$ and $h_{C_i}$ is $C^2$  in $E_i\setminus\{0\}$. The general case follows by approximation, using the weak continuity of mixed area measures with respect to Hausdorff convergence. For the proof we will denote $c_{d_0,\dots,d_p}:=\binom{n-1}{d_0-1,\ldots,d_p-1}$.

Let us first consider the case where the subspaces $V_i$ are mutually orthogonal. Then $|\det J|=1$. By \eqref{eq:MDrep},
for $u\in\mathbb S^{n-1}_+$ we have
$$
\frac{d\operatorname{S}_{C_0[d_0-1],\ldots,C_p[d_p-1]}}{d\mathcal H^{n-1}}(u)
=
\operatorname{D}_{n-1}\bigl(
D^2h_{C_0}(u)[d_0-1],\ldots,D^2h_{C_p}(u)[d_p-1]
\bigr).
$$
Applying Lemmas \ref{lem2.5} and \ref{lem4.1} to the right-hand side, we obtain
$$
c_{d_0,\dots,d_p}
\operatorname{D}_{n-1}\bigl(
D^2h_{C_0}(u)[d_0-1],\ldots,D^2h_{C_p}(u)[d_p-1]
\bigr)=
|\det T|^2
\prod_{i=0}^p
\frac{\det\left(
D^2_{E_i}h_{C_i}(u_i)
\right)}{\|P_{E_i}u\|^{d_i-1}},
$$
where $T:u^\perp\to\bigoplus_{i=0}^p(E_i\cap u^\perp) $ is defined by $Tx=(P_{E_i\cap u^\perp}x)_{i=0}^p$.
We claim that
\begin{align}
\label{eq:detT}
|\det T|=\frac{\langle u,w\rangle^p}{\prod_{i=0}^p\|P_{E_i}u\|}.
\end{align}
Indeed, the adjoint $T^t$ of $T$ is the addition map $T^t(x_0,\dots, x_p)=x_0+\cdots+ x_p$ and the linear map $P_{w^\perp}\circ T^t:\bigoplus_{i=0}^p(E_i\cap u^\perp)\to\bigoplus_{i=0}^p V_i$ is block diagonal. Since $w\in E_i$, the $i$-th block is the orthogonal projection $P_{w^\perp}:(P_{E_i}u)^\perp\to w^\perp$, where the orthogonal complements are taken inside $E_i$, and hence has determinant $|\det P_{w^\perp}|=\frac{\langle P_{E_i}u,  w\rangle}{\|P_{E_i}u\|}=\frac{\langle u,  w\rangle}{\|P_{E_i}u\|}$ by Lemma \ref{lem:detP}. Therefore, 
 $$
\left|\det(P_{w^\perp}\circ T^t)\right|=\prod_{i=0}^p\frac{\langle u,w\rangle}{\|P_{E_i}u\|}
=\frac{\langle u,w\rangle^{p+1}}{\prod_{i=0}^p\|P_{E_i}u\|}.
$$
At the same time, Lemma \ref{lem:detP} also directly implies
$$
\left|\det(P_{w^\perp}\circ T^t)\right|=\left|\det (P_{w^\perp}|_{u^\perp})\right||\det (T)| = \langle u,w\rangle|\det T|.
$$
Combining the two equations shows \eqref{eq:detT}. Consequently,
\begin{align}
\label{eq:LPF1}
c_{d_0,\dots,d_p} d\operatorname{S}_{C_0[d_0-1],\ldots,C_p[d_p-1]}(u)=\langle u,w\rangle^{2p}\prod_{i=0}^p\frac{\det\left(
D^2_{E_i}h_{C_i}(u_i)
\right)}{\|P_{E_i}u\|^{d_i+1}}d\mathcal H^{n-1}(u).
\end{align}
It remains to compute the Jacobian of $\pi$. To this end, for any $x\in u^\perp$ we have
$$
D\pi(u)x=\left(\frac{P_{E_i\cap u^\perp}x}{\|P_{E_i}u\|}\right)_{i=0}^p.
$$
That is, $D\pi(u)$ is the product of $T$ and a block diagonal matrix and thus \eqref{eq:detT} implies
$$
|\det D\pi(u)|
=|\det T|\prod_{i=0}^p\|P_{E_i}u\|^{-(d_i-1)}
=\frac{\langle u,w\rangle^p}{\prod_{i=0}^p\|P_{E_i}u\|^{d_i}}.
$$
Since $\langle u_i,w\rangle=\frac{\langle u,w\rangle}{\|P_{E_i}u\|}$, the change of variables formula and \eqref{eq:MDrep} inside each $E_i$ yield
\begin{align}
\label{eq:LPF2}
&\pi^*\left(\bigotimes_{i=0}^p\langle u_i,w\rangle\,d\operatorname{S}^{E_i}_{C_i}(u_i)\right)=
\langle u,w\rangle^{2p+1}\prod_{i=0}^p\frac{\det\left(D^2_{E_i}h_{C_i}(u_i)\right)}{\|P_{E_i}u\|^{d_i+1}}
\,d\mathcal H^{n-1}(u).
\end{align}
Comparing \eqref{eq:LPF1} with \eqref{eq:LPF2} proves the proposition in the orthogonal case.

If the subspaces $V_i=E_i\cap w^\perp$ are not necessarily orthogonal, choose an invertible linear map $A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ fixing $w$, whose restriction to each $E_i$ is an isometry, and such that the subspaces $A(E_i\cap w^\perp)$ are mutually orthogonal.
Since $A|_{w^\perp}\circ J^t$ is an isometry, we have $|\det A||\det J|=1$. For 
$u\in\mathbb S^{n-1}_+$ set $\phi(u):=\frac{A^{-t}u}{\|A^{-t}u\|}$. 
By \eqref{eq:area-covariance} and $\langle\phi(u),w\rangle=\frac{\langle u,w\rangle}{\|A^{-t}u\|}$, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq22}
\langle\phi(u),w\rangle\,d\left(\phi^*\operatorname{S}_{AC_0[d_0-1],\dots,AC_p[d_p-1]}\right)(u)
=|\det A|\langle u,w\rangle\,d\operatorname{S}_{C_0[d_0-1],\dots,C_p[d_p-1]}(u).
\end{equation}
Let $\pi_A(u):=\left(\frac{P_{AE_iu}}{\|P_{AE_iu}\|}\right)_{i=0}^p$ denote the projection map for the subspaces $AE_i$. Then, by the orthogonal case, the left-hand side of \eqref{eq22} is equal to
$$
c_{d_0,\dots,d_p}^{-1}\phi^*\pi_A^*\left(\bigotimes_{i=0}^p\langle v_i,w\rangle\,d\operatorname{S}^{AE_i}_{AC_i}(v_i)\right)=c_{d_0,\dots,d_p}^{-1}\pi^*\left(\bigotimes_{i=0}^p\langle u_i,w\rangle\,d\operatorname{S}^{E_i}_{C_i}(u_i)\right),
$$
where we used $\pi_A\circ\phi=(A,\dots,A)\circ\pi$, which follows from $P_{AE_i}A^{-t}u=AP_{E_i}u$, and \eqref{eq:area-covariance} again for the isometries $A|_{E_i}$. Now \eqref{eq25} follows at once using $|\det A|^{-1}=|\det J|$.

label: eq10
title: Proof
body_md:
We will keep the notation from the proof of Proposition \ref{pro:higherGodbersen}. In particular, $N=(p+1)n$, and $\widetilde\iota_0,\dots,\widetilde\iota_p:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^N$ are the canonical inclusions. By \eqref{eq:higherGproof1} and \eqref{eq:higherGproof2}, a full-dimensional convex body $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ attains equality in \eqref{eq:higher-godbersen} if and only if
$$
\begin{aligned}
&\operatorname{V}_N\bigl(\Delta_{p+1}K[n],\widetilde\iota_0K[n-k_0],\dots,\widetilde\iota_pK[n-k_p]\bigr)\\
&\qquad=\operatorname{V}_N\bigl(K^{p+1}[n],\widetilde\iota_0K[n-k_0],\dots,\widetilde\iota_pK[n-k_p]\bigr)>0.
\end{aligned}
$$
By Lemma \ref{lem2.11}, this is equivalent to
\begin{equation}
h_{\Delta_{p+1}K}=h_{K^{p+1}}\quad\text{on}\quad\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-1],\widetilde\iota_0K[n-k_0],\dots,\widetilde\iota_pK[n-k_p]},
\label{eq10}
\end{equation}
where $B$ is the unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^N$.

Assume first that \eqref{eq10} holds and fix nonzero $u_0,\dots,u_p\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\dim T(K,u_i)\leq k_i$. Without loss of generality, we may normalize so that $u:=(u_0,\dots,u_p)\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$.
For each $i$, choose a subspace $E_i\subseteq T(K,u_i)^\perp$ of dimension $n-k_i$ and denote
$$
E:=\left(\bigoplus_{i=0}^p\widetilde\iota_iE_i\right)\oplus\mathbb{R} u,
\qquad E_i':=\widetilde\iota_iE_i\oplus\mathbb{R} u.
$$
Then $\dim E=pn+1$, $\dim E_i'=n-k_i+1$, and the subspaces $E_i'\cap u^\perp=\widetilde\iota_iE_i$ are mutually orthogonal.
Moreover, $P_E\widetilde\iota_iK=P_{E_i'}\widetilde\iota_iK$ is full-dimensional in $E_i'$.
By \eqref{eq7} and the choice of $E_i$, we have
$$
T_{E_i'}(P_{E_i'}\widetilde\iota_iK,u)
=T(\widetilde\iota_iK,u)\cap E_i'
=\mathbb{R}_{\geq0}u.
$$
Indeed, $\widetilde\iota_i x+tu\in T(\widetilde\iota_iK,u)$ with $x\in E_i$ if and only if $x+tu_i\in T(K,u_i)$, which forces $x=0$ and $t\geq0$.
Thus $u$ is a $0$-extreme direction of $P_{E_i'}\widetilde\iota_iK$ for every $i$.
Since the support of the surface area measure is the closure of the $0$-extreme directions \cite[Theorem~4.5.3]{Sch14}, Proposition \ref{prop:local_proj} gives
$$
u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}^E_{P_E\widetilde\iota_0K[n-k_0],\dots,P_E\widetilde\iota_pK[n-k_p]}.
$$
Now $\dim E^\perp=n-1$.
By Corollary \ref{cor2.9}, we obtain
$$
u\in\operatorname{supp}\operatorname{S}_{B[n-1],\widetilde\iota_0K[n-k_0],\dots,\widetilde\iota_pK[n-k_p]}.
$$
By \eqref{eq10}, $h_{\Delta_{p+1}K}(u)=h_{K^{p+1}}(u)$, that is,
$$
\max_{x\in K}\sum_{i=0}^p\langle x,u_i\rangle
=\sum_{i=0}^p\max_{x\in K}\langle x,u_i\rangle.
$$
Any maximizer on the left-hand side thus belongs to $\bigcap_{i=0}^p \{x\in K: \langle x, u_i\rangle = h_K(u_i)\}$.
Choose such a point $x$ and a unit vector $w\in\operatorname{relint} N(K,x)$.
Then $N(K,x)=T(K,w)$ contains every $u_i$, and hence every $T(K,u_i)$, which completes the proof for the ``only if'' direction.

For the ``if'' direction, assume that, conversely, the condition on touching cones holds.
By \cite[Corollary 1.9]{vHW25}, in order  to prove \eqref{eq10}, it suffices to show $h_{\Delta_{p+1}K}(u)=h_{K^{p+1}}(u)$ for every $(B[n-1],\widetilde\iota_0K[n-k_0],\dots,\widetilde\iota_pK[n-k_p])$-extreme direction $u\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$. Let $u=(u_0,\dots,u_p)$ be such a direction. Then, by definition, $\dim T(\widetilde\iota_iK,u)^\perp\geq n-k_i$ for all $i$. Since
$$
T(\widetilde\iota_iK,u)^\perp=\widetilde\iota_i\left(T(K,u_i)^\perp\right),
$$
we have $\dim T(K,u_i)\leq k_i$.
Applying the assumption on touching cones, we obtain $w\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $T(K,w)$ contains every $T(K,u_i)$.
Fix $x\in K$ with $\langle x,w\rangle=h_K(w)$.
Then for every $i$, $u_i\in T(K,w)\subseteq N(K,x)$ and, in particular, $h_K(u_i)=\langle x,u_i\rangle$.
Consequently,
$$
h_{\Delta_{p+1}K}(u)\geq\sum_{i=0}^p\langle x,u_i\rangle=\sum_{i=0}^p h_K(u_i)=h_{K^{p+1}}(u).
$$
Since the reverse inequality holds for any $u\in\mathbb S^{N-1}$ because $\Delta_{p+1}K\subseteq K^{p+1}$, this finishes the proof.

label: lem:T
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:T}
Suppose that $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ satisfies $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$, where $1\leq k\leq n-1$.
Let $F$ and $G$ be  faces of $K$ with $\dim G=n-k$.
If there is a face $T$ of $K$ such that $F\subseteq T$, $\dim T\leq k-1$, and $T\cap G\neq\emptyset$, then $F\vee G$ is proper.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume such $T$ exists. If $T\cap\operatorname{relint} G\neq \emptyset$, then $G\subseteq T$ by Lemma~\ref{lemma2.1}, and the conclusion follows.
Otherwise, choose $y\in T\cap \operatorname{relbd} G$ and $g\in\operatorname{relint} G$. Then there exists  $z\in\operatorname{relbd} G$ such that $g\in(y,z)$. 
Since $z\in\operatorname{relbd} G$, $F(K,z)$ is a proper face of $G$, and hence $\dim F(K,z)\leq n-k-1$.
Property $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$ then implies that $T\vee F(K,z)$ is proper. Since $y,z\in T\vee F(K,z)$, we have $g\in \operatorname{relint} G\cap\big( T\vee F(K,z)\big)$, and Lemma~\ref{lemma2.1} gives $G\subseteq T\vee F(K,z)$.
As $F\subseteq T\vee F(K,z)$ as well, $F\vee G$ is a face of $T\vee F(K,z)$, which is proper.
Therefore $F\vee G$ is a proper face of $K$.

label: lem:2cases
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We fix $u\in\operatorname{relint} F$ and $v\in\operatorname{relint} G$ for the rest of the proof and put $o:=(u+v)/2$.
Then we have $o\in \operatorname{relint} \operatorname{conv}(F,G)$. If $o\in\partial K$, we can find a proper face $H$ of $K$ containing $o$. Then $u,v\in H$, and Lemma~\ref{lemma2.1} implies that $H$ must also contain $F$ and $G$. Therefore $F\vee G\subseteq  H$ is a proper face of $K$, and item (a) holds in this case. 
In the following we will assume $o\in \operatorname{int} K$ and aim to prove the second claim. We will denote $S:=\operatorname{aff}(F, G)$ and $Q:=\operatorname{conv}(F, G)$.

To prove that $F$ and $G$ are affinely independent, we must show $\dim S=\dim F+\dim G+1$. To this end, we consider the convex body
$$
\widehat Q:=\left\{((1-t)f,tg,t):f\in F,\ g\in G,\ 0\leq t\leq1\right\}\in\mathcal{K}^{2n+1},
$$
i.e., the convex hull of $F\times\{0\}\times\{0\}$ and $\{0\}\times G\times\{1\}$, and the linear map $\pi:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^n$ given by $\pi(a,b,t):=a+b$. Observe that $\pi(\widehat Q)=Q$, hence $\pi(\operatorname{aff}\widehat Q)=S$. Because $\dim \operatorname{aff}\widehat Q=\dim F+\dim G+1$, it suffices to show that $\pi|_{\operatorname{aff}\widehat Q}$ is injective.


We will first show that $\pi(\operatorname{relbd}\widehat Q)\subseteq\partial K$. We have
$$
\operatorname{relbd} \widehat Q=R_1\cup R_2\cup \left(\bigcup_{f\in\operatorname{relbd} F}R_{3,f}\right)\cup\left(\bigcup_{g\in\operatorname{relbd} G}R_{4,g}\right),
$$
where 
\begin{align*}
    R_1&:=F\times\{0\}\times\{0\},\\
    R_2&:=\{0\}\times G\times\{1\},\\
    R_{3,f}&:=\left\{\big((1-t)f,tg,t\big):0<t<1, \,g\in G\right\},\quad f\in\operatorname{relbd} F,\\
    R_{4,g}&:=\left\{\big((1-t)f,tg,t\big):0<t<1,\, f\in F\right\}, \quad g\in\operatorname{relbd} G.
\end{align*}
Since  $F$ and $G$ are proper faces of $K$, $\pi(R_1)$ and $\pi(R_2)$ are contained in $\partial K$. Since every $f\in\operatorname{relbd} F$ lies in a proper face $F'$ of $F$, \eqref{eq:subface_property_F} implies $\pi(R_{3,f})\subseteq F'\vee G\subseteq\partial K$. Similarly, using \eqref{eq:subface_property_G}, we get $\pi(R_{4,g})\subseteq\partial K$ for every $g\in\operatorname{relbd} G$. 
We thus conclude $\pi(\operatorname{relbd}\widehat Q)\subseteq\partial K$.


Consider the point $\widehat o:=(u/2,v/2,1/2)\in\operatorname{relint}\widehat Q$. It satisfies  $\pi(\widehat o)=o$.
Fix an arbitrary nonzero  $w\in \mathbb{R}^n\times \mathbb{R}^n\times \mathbb{R}$ such that $\widehat o+ w\in \operatorname{aff}\widehat Q$.
Then the ray  $\{\widehat o+tw$: $t\in (0,+ \infty)\}$ intersects the relative boundary of $\widehat Q$.
That is,  there is $r>0$ such that $\widehat o+rw\in\operatorname{relbd}\widehat Q$.
Using $\pi(\operatorname{relbd}\widehat Q)\subseteq\partial K$, we obtain $\pi(\widehat o+rw) \in \partial K$.
But $\pi(\widehat o) = o  \in \operatorname{int} K$.
Therefore, $\pi(w) = r^{-1}(\pi(\widehat o+rw) - \pi(\widehat o))\neq 0$.
Since $w$ was chosen arbitrarily,  $\pi$ is injective on $\operatorname{aff}\widehat Q$.
We have thus proven that $F$ and $G$ are affinely independent.


For the  claim $K\cap S = Q$, note first that $K\cap S\supseteq Q$ holds because $S = \operatorname{aff} Q$.
For the reverse inclusion, assume for contradiction that there exists $x\in (K\cap S)\setminus Q$.
In particular,   $x\in \operatorname{aff} Q\setminus Q $.
Since $o\in \operatorname{relint} Q$, the open segment $(o,x)$ intersects $\operatorname{relbd} Q\subseteq\partial K$ at some point $y$.
However, since $o\in \operatorname{int} K$ and $x\in K$, we have $(o,x)\subseteq \operatorname{int} K$, a contradiction.
We thus conclude  $K\cap S = Q$.

Finally, choose an extreme point $y\in G$ and set $D:=F\vee y$. To prove \eqref{eq:convFy}, observe first that both sides are faces of $\operatorname{conv} (F,G)$. Indeed, on the one hand, $\operatorname{conv}(F,y)\subseteq\operatorname{conv} (F,G)$ is a face since $y$ is an extreme point of $G$.
On the other hand, $D$ is a face of $K$, so $D\cap S$ is a face of $K\cap S=\operatorname{conv}(F,G)$. Next, put $p:=(u+y)/2$.
Since $y\notin\operatorname{aff} F$, we have $p\in\operatorname{relint} \operatorname{conv}(F,y)$. By Lemma~\ref{lemma2.2}, $p$ also lies in $\operatorname{relint} D$ and hence in $\operatorname{relint}(D\cap S)$. Consequently, $\operatorname{relint} (D\cap S) \cap \operatorname{relint} \operatorname{conv}(F,y)\neq \emptyset$. Now Lemma \ref{lemma2.1} applied twice implies $D\cap S= \operatorname{conv}(F,y)$, as claimed.

label: lemma4.5
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma4.5}
Let $2\leq k\leq n-1$, and suppose that $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ satisfies $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$.
Let $F$ and $G$ be faces of $K$ with $\dim F=k$ and $\dim G=n-k$, such that $F\cap G=\{y\}$ for some $y\in K$ and $\operatorname{aff}(F, G)=\mathbb{R}^n$.
Then $\operatorname{conv}(F,G)=K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Translate $K$ so that $y=0$. Then $U:=\operatorname{aff} F$ and $V:=\operatorname{aff} G$ are complementary linear subspaces, that is, $\mathbb{R}^n=U\oplus V$. In particular, $\dim\operatorname{conv}(F,G)=n$. Since $\operatorname{conv}(F,G)\subseteq K$ it suffices to show $\partial (\operatorname{conv}(F,G))\subseteq\partial K$.

Observe that we in fact have $0\in\operatorname{relbd} F\cap\operatorname{relbd} G$.
Indeed, if for instance $0\in \operatorname{relint} F$, Lemma \ref{lemma2.1} implies that $F\subseteq G$, and  hence $U$ and $V$ cannot be linearly independent.


We claim that every point $z\in\partial (\operatorname{conv}(F,G))$ lies in a segment $[f,g]$ with $f\in\operatorname{relbd} F$ and $g\in\operatorname{relbd} G$.
The case $z=0$ is immediate, since $0\in\operatorname{relbd} F\cap\operatorname{relbd} G$.
If $z\in F\setminus\{0\}$, the ray from $0$ through $z$ intersects $\operatorname{relbd} F$ at $f$.
Then $z\in[0,f]$ as required.
The case $z\in G\setminus\{0\}$  follows similarly.
Otherwise, write $z=tf_0+(1-t)g_0$ with $0<t<1$, $f_0\in F$, and $g_0\in G$.
If $f_0\in \operatorname{relbd} F$ and $g_0\in \operatorname{relbd} G$, we are already done.
Hence we assume for example $f_0\in \operatorname{relint} F$.
Let $H$ be a proper face of $\operatorname{conv}(F,G)$ containing $z$.
Then $f_0,g_0\in H$, and in particular $f_0 \in H\cap \operatorname{relint} F$.
By  Lemma~\ref{lemma2.1},  $F\subseteq H$.
So $0\in H$ and $H\cap G$ is a proper face of $G$.
Extend the ray from $0$ through $f_0$ to $f\in\operatorname{relbd} F$, and write $f_0=\rho f$ with $0<\rho<1$.
Set $g:=\frac{1-t}{1-t\rho}g_0$.
Then $g\in[0,g_0]\subseteq H\cap G\subseteq\operatorname{relbd} G$ and $z=t\rho f+(1-t\rho)g$. This shows the existence of $f\in \operatorname{relbd} F,\, g\in \operatorname{relbd} G $ with $z\in [f,g]$ in this case. The case $g_0\in\operatorname{relint} G$ is analogous.



Fix $z\in \partial (\operatorname{conv}(F,G))$ and choose $f,g$ as above.
Since $f\in \operatorname{relbd} F$, we have $\dim F(K,f)\leq\dim F-1 = k-1$.
Similarly, $\dim F(K,g)\leq n-k-1$.
Property $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$ therefore implies that $f,g$ are contained in a proper face of $K$.
In particular, $z\in [f,g]\subseteq F(K, \{f,g\})\subseteq\partial K$.
Since $z$ was chosen arbitrarily, we conclude $\partial (\operatorname{conv}(F,G))\subseteq\partial K$.

label: lemma4.6
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lemma4.6}
Let $1\leq k\leq n-1$, and let $D,G\in \mathcal{K}^n$ with $\dim D=k$ and $\dim G=n-k$, such that $0 \in D\cap G$ and $D\cup G$ spans $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Let $F$ be a face of $D$ with $0 \notin F$.
Then there is a face $T$ of $\operatorname{conv}(D,G)$ containing $F$, meeting $G$, and satisfying $\dim T=\dim F+1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $C:=\operatorname{conv}(D,G)$, $U:=\operatorname{aff} D$, and $V:=\operatorname{aff} G$.
Since $0\in D\cap G$, the hypotheses give $\mathbb{R}^n=U\oplus V$.
Choose a nonzero extreme point $w$ of $G$, and set $T:=\operatorname{conv}(F,w)$.
Our choice of $w$ implies $w\in T\cap G$ and $w\notin U$, so $\dim T=\dim F+1$.


To verify the face property, suppose $z\in T$ and $z=\lambda x_1+(1-\lambda)x_2$, where $x_1,x_2\in C$, $0<\lambda<1$. We need to show that $x_1,x_2\in T$.



Write $x_i=\alpha_i d_i+(1-\alpha_i)g_i$, where $d_i\in D$, $g_i\in G$, and $0\leq\alpha_i\leq1$, for $i=1,2$. Put $r:=\lambda\alpha_1+(1-\lambda)\alpha_2$. 
Since $z\in T$, we also have $z=t f+(1-t)w$, for some $f\in F$ and $0\leq t\leq1$.
Together, we have
$$
t f+(1-t)w =z = \lambda (\alpha_1 d_1+(1-\alpha_1)g_1)+(1-\lambda)(\alpha_2 d_2+(1-\alpha_2)g_2).
$$
Taking the components in $U$ and $V$ respectively gives
\begin{align}
\label{eq11}
t f
&=\lambda\alpha_1d_1+(1-\lambda)\alpha_2d_2,\\
(1-t)w
&=\lambda(1-\alpha_1)g_1+(1-\lambda)(1-\alpha_2)g_2.
\label{eq12}
\end{align}
We claim that this implies $r=t$. Indeed, if $r<t$, then \eqref{eq11} implies
$$
f
=\frac{\lambda\alpha_1}{t}d_1
+\frac{(1-\lambda)\alpha_2}{t}d_2
+\left(1-\frac rt\right)0.
$$
Hence $f$ is a convex combination of points where $0$ has a positive coefficient.
Since $f\in F$, we have $0\in F$, a contradiction. If $r>t$, then \eqref{eq12} implies
\[
w=\frac{\lambda(1-\alpha_1)}{1-t}g_1
+\frac{(1-\lambda)(1-\alpha_2)}{1-t}g_2
+\frac{r-t}{1-t}0.
\]
However, $w$ is an extreme point, hence cannot be written as a nontrivial convex combination of points in $G$, a contradiction. We thus have $r=t$ and will distinguish three cases.

First, if $t=0$, then $r=0$ forces $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=0$. Thus $x_1,x_2\in G$, and \eqref{eq12} together with extremality of $w$ in $G$ gives $x_1=x_2=w\in T$.


Second, if $t=1$, then $r=1$ forces $\alpha_1=\alpha_2=1$. Thus $x_1,x_2\in D$, and \eqref{eq11} together with the face property of $F$ in $D$ gives $x_1,x_2\in F\subseteq T$.

Finally, assume $0<t<1$. Then by \eqref{eq11} and \eqref{eq12} we have the convex combinations
\begin{align}
\label{eq11convex}
f &=\frac{\lambda\alpha_1}{t}d_1 +\frac{(1-\lambda)\alpha_2}{t}d_2,\\
w&=\frac{\lambda(1-\alpha_1)}{1-t}g_1 +\frac{(1-\lambda)(1-\alpha_2)}{1-t}g_2.
\label{eq12convex}
\end{align}
If $\alpha_i>0$, then \eqref{eq11convex} together with the face property of $F$ in $D$ implies $d_i\in F$. If $\alpha_i<1$, then \eqref{eq12convex} together with extremality of $w$ in $G$ implies $g_i=w$. An easy case distinction then shows that $x_i=\alpha_i d_i+(1-\alpha_i)g_i\in\operatorname{conv}(F,w)$, $i=1,2$, for any $(\alpha_1,\alpha_2)\in[0,1]^2$.

label: lem:with_subface
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:with_subface}
    Let $2\leq k\leq n-1$ and $0\leq d\leq k-2$. Let $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body satisfying $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$. Assume that $F$ and $G$ are faces of $K$ satisfying $\dim F=d$, $\dim G=n-k$, and \eqref{eq:subface_property_F}. Then $F\vee G$ is proper.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $G'$ be a proper face of $G$. Then $\dim G'\leq n-k-1$ and $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$ implies that $F\vee G'$ is proper. Hence, $F$ and $G$ also satisfy \eqref{eq:subface_property_G} and we may use Lemma \ref{lem:2cases}. If item (a) in Lemma~\ref{lem:2cases} holds, then we are done. 
Therefore, we assume from now on that item (b) holds. Choose an extreme point $y$ of $G$ and denote $D:=F\vee y$. We will also denote $S:=\operatorname{aff}(F,G)$. Then $F$ and $G$ are affinely independent, $K\cap S = \operatorname{conv} (F, G)$, and $D\cap S = \operatorname{conv}(F,y)$.

Property $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$ implies that $D$ is proper. Moreover, since $F$ and $G$ are affinely independent, we have
\begin{align*}
    \dim S &= \dim F+\dim G+1 = d+n-k+1,\\
    \dim \operatorname{conv}(F,y) &= \dim F+1 = d+1,
\end{align*}
and therefore
\begin{equation}\label{eq13}
\dim D\leq \dim (D\cap S)+\operatorname{codim}(S) = 
\dim\operatorname{conv}(F,y)+n-\dim S=k.
\end{equation}
If $\dim D\leq k-1$, then taking $T=D$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:T} shows that $F\vee G$ is proper as desired. 


It remains to treat the case $\dim D=k$. In this case, \eqref{eq13} takes equality, which yields $\operatorname{aff} (D,S)=\mathbb{R}^n$. Since $F\subseteq D$ and $S=\operatorname{aff}(F,G)$, we have $\operatorname{aff}(D, G)=\mathbb{R}^n$.
Moreover, $D\cap G=\operatorname{conv}(F,y)\cap G=\{y\}$.
We may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lemma4.5} to $D,G$, which  gives $K=\operatorname{conv}(D,G)$. Since $F$ is a proper face of $D$ and translating $K$ so that $y=0$, Lemma~\ref{lemma4.6} implies that there is a face $T$ of $K$ containing $F$, intersecting $G$, and satisfying $\dim T=d+1\leq k-1$. Applying Lemma~\ref{lem:T} to this $T$ shows that $F\vee G$ is proper.
head: environment

label: lem:without_subface
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:without_subface}
    Let $2\leq k\leq n-1$ and $0\leq d\leq k-2$. Let $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body satisfying $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$. Assume that $F$ and $G$ are faces of $K$ satisfying $\dim F=d$ and $\dim G=n-k$. Then $F\vee G$ is proper.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We argue by strong induction on $d$. First, if $d=0$, then there is no proper face of $F$. Hence \eqref{eq:subface_property_F} holds trivially and the claim follows immediately from Lemma \ref{lem:with_subface}. Second, fix $d>0$ and assume the statement holds for $0,\dots,d-1$. For every proper face $F'$ of $F$, we have $\dim F'<d$ and hence the induction hypothesis implies that $F'\vee G$ is proper. Thus \eqref{eq:subface_property_F} holds and the claim follows again from  Lemma \ref{lem:with_subface}.

label: prop4.8
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop4.8}
Let $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body and $2\leq k\leq n-1$. If $K$ satisfies $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$, then it satisfies $(I_{k-2,n-k})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Take any faces $F,G$ of $K$ with $\dim F\leq k-2$ and $\dim G\leq n-k$. If $\dim G\leq n-k-1$, property $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$ gives that $F\vee G$ is proper. Otherwise, $\dim G=n-k$, and the same conclusion follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:without_subface}, applied with $d=\dim F$. Since $F$ and $G$ were arbitrary, $K$ satisfies $(I_{k-2,n-k})$.
head: environment

label: lem:induction_base
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:induction_base}
Let $K\in\mathcal{K}^n$ be a full-dimensional convex body. If $K$ satisfies $(I_{0,n-2})$, then $K$ is a simplex.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x$ be an arbitrary extreme point of $K$ and put $F:=\{x\}$. Choose $p\in\operatorname{int} K$ and let $b\in\partial K$ be the (unique) point such that $p\in[b,x]$. Denote $G:=F(K,b)$.
Then $F\vee G$ contains $p\in \operatorname{int} K$ and thus $F\vee G=K$.
Since $K$ satisfies $(I_{0,n-2})$,  we have  $\dim G=n-1$. Moreover, for any proper face $G'$ of $G$, one has $\dim G'\leq n-2$ and hence by $(I_{0,n-2})$, $F\vee G'$ is proper. This shows that \eqref{eq:subface_property_G} holds. Note also that \eqref{eq:subface_property_F} holds trivially since $F$ has no proper faces.
We may therefore apply Lemma~\ref{lem:2cases}. 
Since  $F\vee G=K$, item (a) of Lemma~\ref{lem:2cases} cannot hold. 
Hence $F$ and $G$ are affinely independent and one has
$$
K = K\cap \operatorname{aff}(F,G) =\operatorname{conv}(F,G) = \operatorname{conv} (G,x).
$$
We thus conclude that $K$ is a pyramid with base $G$ and apex $x$.
In particular, every extreme point of $K$ other than $x$ belongs to $G$ and so $x$ does not lie in the affine hull of the other extreme points.

Since $x$ was arbitrary, we get that every finite set of extreme points of $K$ is affinely independent and consequently $K$ has at most $n+1$ extreme points. Since $K$ is full-dimensional and equal to the convex hull of its extreme points, we conclude that $K$ is an $n$-simplex.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First, assume that $K$ satisfies (b) or, in other words, the property $(I_{k-1,n-k-1})$. Applying Proposition~\ref{prop4.8} repeatedly, this implies that $K$ satisfies $(I_{0,n-2})$. 
Now Lemma~\ref{lem:induction_base} shows that $K$ is a simplex.

Conversely, assume that $K$ is a simplex and $F,G$ are faces of $K$ with $\dim F\leq k-1$ and $\dim G\leq n-k-1$. Since $F$ and $G$ are simplices themselves, they together contain at most $k+(n-k)=n$ vertices of $K$. Hence there is a vertex $y\in K$ not contained in $F\cup G$. Choose $H$ to be the facet of $K$ not containing $y$. Then $F\vee G\subseteq H$ and (b) follows. 

Next, translate $K$ so that it contains the origin in its interior and assume that $K^{\circ}$ satisfies (b). Consider $u, v\in\mathbb S^{n-1}$ such that $\dim T(K, u)\leq k$ and $\dim T(K, v)\leq n-k$. By Lemma \ref{lem:fact}, $F:=T(K, u)\cap\partial K^{\circ}$ and $G:=T(K, v)\cap\partial K^{\circ}$ are faces of $K^\circ$ satisfying $\dim F\leq k-1$ and $\dim G\leq n-k-1$. Therefore, the face $F\vee G$ is proper. Using Lemma  \ref{lem:fact}, we have $\mathbb R_{\geq0}(F\vee G)=T(K, w)$ for some $w\in\mathbb S^{n-1}$. The touching cone $T(K, w)$ clearly contains both $T(K, u)$ and $T(K, v)$, and we conclude that $K$ satisfies (c).

Conversely, assume that $K$ satisfies (c), and let $F, G$ be proper faces of $K^{\circ}$ such that $\dim F\leq k-1$ and $\dim G\leq n-k-1$. By Lemma \ref{lem:fact}, there exist $u, v\in\mathbb S^{n-1}$ with $\mathbb R_{\geq0}F=T(K, u)$ and $\mathbb R_{\geq0}G=T(K, v)$. Then $\dim T(K, u)\leq k$ and $\dim T(K, v)\leq n-k$, and hence condition (c) in turn ensures that there exists some $w\in\mathbb S^{n-1}$ such that $T(K, w)$ contains both $T(K, u)$ and $T(K, v)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:fact}, $T(K, w)\cap\partial K^{\circ}$ is a proper face of $K^\circ$. Since it clearly contains both $F$ and $G$, $F\vee G$ is proper. We conclude that $K^{\circ}$ satisfies (b). 

Finally, observing that $K\in\mathcal{K}^n_o$ is a simplex if and only if $K^{\circ}$ is a simplex and using the previously shown equivalence (a)$\iff$(b), we have that $K$ satisfies (c) if and only if $K$ is a simplex. This finishes the proof.

head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Without loss of generality we may assume $f+g = n+1$. 
    We will inductively construct two sequences  $(F_j)$ and $(G_j)$, $j=0,1,\dots$, of proper faces of $K$ satisfying $F_j\vee G_j=K$, $\dim F_j\leq f-1$ and \eqref{eq:subface_property_F},  \eqref{eq:subface_property_G} from Lemma \ref{lem:2cases}.
    
First, we may always write $K = x_1 \vee \dots \vee x_m $ where $m$ is an integer and $x_1,\dots,x_m$ are extreme points of $K$. Let us fix such a representation of $K$ with minimal $m$. We let $F_0 := \{x_1\}$ and $G_0$  be a minimal face of $x_2 \vee \dots \vee x_m$ such that $F_0\vee G_0=K$. It is clear that $F_0,G_0$ are faces of $K$ with the required properties.

Second, assume that $F_j,G_j\subseteq K$ are as above. If $\dim G_j\leq g-1$, we set $F_{j+1}:=F_j$ and $G_{j+1}:=G_j$. If $\dim G_j\geq g$, we proceed as follows: Pick a maximal proper face $\widetilde G\subseteq G_j$. Then there exists an extreme point $y\in G_j$ not contained in $\widetilde G$. We set $\widetilde F:=F_j\vee y$. By Lemma \ref{lem:2cases}, $F_j$ and $G_j$ are affinely independent and satisfy \eqref{eq:convFy}. The former implies
$$
\dim\operatorname{aff}(F_j, G_j) = \dim F_j + \dim G_j + 1,
$$
the latter yields $\operatorname{aff}(\widetilde F\cap\operatorname{aff}(F_j, G_j))=\operatorname{aff}(F_j,y)$. Consequently,
\begin{align*}
    \dim \widetilde F&\leq\dim\operatorname{aff}(\widetilde F\cap\operatorname{aff}(F_j,G_j))+\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{aff}(F_j,G_j)\\
    &=\dim F_j+1+n-(\dim F_j+\dim G_j+1)\\
    &=n-\dim G_j\\
    &\leq f-1,
    \end{align*}
where in the last step we used our assumptions $f+g=n+1$ and $\dim G_j\geq g$. Using the maximality of $\widetilde G$, we further have
$$
\widetilde F\vee \widetilde G=F_j\vee y\vee \widetilde G=F_j\vee G_j=K.
$$
We choose faces $F_{j+1}\subseteq \widetilde F$ and $G_{j+1}\subseteq \widetilde G$ satisfying $F_{j+1}\vee G_{j+1}=K$ and minimizing $\dim F_{j+1}+\dim G_{j+1}$. Then we have $\dim F_{j+1}\leq \dim\widetilde F\leq f-1$, and the minimality of $\dim F_{j+1}+\dim G_{j+1}$ implies that $F_{j+1},G_{j+1}$ satisfy \eqref{eq:subface_property_F} and \eqref{eq:subface_property_G}. Note that $F_{j+1},G_{j+1}$ are clearly proper faces of $K$ since $F_j,G_j$ were such.



 Observe that, if $\dim G_j\geq g$, we have $\dim G_{j+1}<\dim G_j$ since $\widetilde G\subseteq G_j$ was proper. Therefore, there exists $j_0\geq0$ such that $\dim G_{j_0}\leq g-1$ and we thus may take $F:=F_{j_0}$ and $G:=G_{j_0}$ to finish the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $K$ satisfies $(I_{q_0,\dots, q_p})$ and consider any faces $F_0,\dots,F_{p-1}\subseteq K$ with
    $$\dim F_i\leq q_i,\quad i=0,\dots,p-2,\qquad\text{and}\qquad \dim F_{p-1}\leq q_{p-1}+q_p+1.
    $$
    By Proposition \ref{pro:reduction_higher_godbersen}, there exist faces $F,G\subseteq F_{p-1}$ such that $\dim F\leq q_{p-1}$, $\dim G\leq q_p$, and $F\vee G=F_{p-1}$. By $(I_{q_0,\dots, q_p})$, $
    F_0\vee\cdots\vee F_{p-1}=F_0\vee\cdots\vee F_{p-2}\vee F\vee G
    $
    is a proper face of $K$, and hence $K$ satisfies $(I_{q_0,\dots,q_{p-2},q_{p-1}+q_p+1})$.

First, assume that $K$ satisfies (b) or, in other words, the property $(I_{k_0-1,\dots, k_p-1})$. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:p_reduction} repeatedly and using $\sum_{i=0}^pk_i=n$, this implies that $K$ satisfies $(I_{k_0-1,n-k_0-1})$. 
Now Theorem \ref{thm:equivalent} implies that $K$ is a simplex.

Conversely, assume that $K$ is a simplex and $F_0,\dots,F_p$ are faces of $K$ with $\dim F_i\leq k_i-1$, $i=0,\dots,p$. Since $F_0,\dots,F_p$ are simplices themselves, they together contain at most $\sum_{i=0}^p k_i=n$ vertices of $K$. Hence there is a vertex $y\in K$ not contained in any $F_i$, $i=0,\dots,p$. Choosing $F\subseteq K$ to be the facet not containing $y$, (b) follows. 

Finally, translate $K$ so that it contains the origin in its interior. Then a straightforward generalization of the corresponding part of the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:equivalent}, that is, an easy application of Lemma \ref{lem:fact}, shows that $K$ satisfies (c) if and only if $K^\circ$ satisfies (b). By the previously shown equivalence (a)$\iff$(b), we thus have that $K$ satisfies (c) if and only if $K^\circ$ is a simplex. Using the self-duality property of a simplex, we conclude that (a)$\iff$(c). This finishes the proof.
